title: Paramount Network Orders 13 Original Episodes of Larry the Cable Guy-Hosted Clip Show ‘American Mayhem’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: “American Mayhem,” the new syndicated half-hour clip series hosted by Larry the Cable Guy, is getting a linear cable platform as well. Paramount Ne
body:
“American Mayhem,” the new syndicated half-hour clip series hosted by Larry the Cable Guy, is getting a linear cable platform as well. Paramount Network has ordered 13 episodes of “American Mayhem” from producer V10 Entertainment.

	The 13 episodes, which will launch Friday, Nov. 13, at 9 p.m. ET, will be new and original to Paramount Network. The deal is separate from the 52-episode syndicated version of “American Mayhem” distributed to stations by CBS Media Ventures. 
	

	Here’s the logline for “American Mayhem”: “With his signature heartland humor, Larry the Cable Guy guides viewers through a fast-paced collection of funny, unexpected and relatable moments captured across America. From backyard mishaps and weekend DIY disasters to pets stealing the spotlight and celebrations that don’t go as planned, ‘American Mayhem’ finds the humor in everyday life, with clips spanning small towns, ball fields, family gatherings and more.”

	“‘American Mayhem’ reflects the humor and unpredictability of everyday life in an entertaining way,” said Laurel Weir, head of programming and acquisitions for Paramount Media Networks and chief research and insights officer for TV Media, in a statement. “Larry the Cable Guy is the perfect comedian to bring these moments to life, with his natural ability to connect with audiences. We’re excited to partner with V10 Entertainment to bring this new format to Paramount Network with a host whose voice and perspective make it distinctly his own.”

	“American Mayhem” is executive produced by Larry The Cable Guy, Maggie Houlehan, Carter Skeath, Rick De Oliveira, Josh Vodnoy and John Stevens. The syndicated version of “American Mayhem” is cleared across major markets including WLNY New York, KCAL Los Angeles and WCIU Chicago.
	

	“Larry doesn’t just make people laugh; he understands the people he’s making laugh, and that’s what makes him so uniquely suited for ‘American Mayhem,’” said V10 Entertainment president Carter Skeath in a statement. “The show embraces the funny, unpredictable, rough-and-tumble side of Americana that feels right at home on Paramount Network. It’s also another opportunity to build on a partnership we genuinely value with an incredible team at Skydance.”

	Added Larry the Cable Guy, in a statement: “I watch a ton of the shows on Paramount Network and to see ‘Mayhem’ premiere on their platform is something I’m really excited about — nothing celebrates this country like watching somebody’s uncle fall through a lawn chair.”

title: Bradley Cooper and Danny McBride’s ‘G.I. Joe’ Movie Set for 2028; Paramount Shifts New ‘Paranormal Activity’ to Halloween 2027

body:
Danny McBride‘s “G.I. Joe” movie, starring Bradley Cooper, will march into movie theaters in 2028.

	Paramount announced on Friday that the film will get a wide theatrical release on Oct. 20, 2028. McBride will direct the reimagining of the “G.I. Joe” franchise — which kicked off with the Hasbro toy line and spawned comic book series, animated series and a trio of live-action films — from a screenplay he wrote with Jeff Fradley and John Carcieri. Cooper is set to star as Duke, one of the franchise’s most iconic characters, but the studio is keeping further plot details under wraps. The film is produced by Lorenzo di Bonaventura, Mark Vahradian, and Zev Foreman for Hasbro Entertainment.
	

	The studio also revealed that the next “Paranormal Activity” movie will debut in the Halloween corridor (on October 22, 2027), instead of launching in the summer. (The Paramount and Blumhouse Atomic film, directed by Ian Tuason, was previously dated for May 21.)

	Created by Oren Peli, the original “Paranormal Activity” grossed nearly $194 million worldwide and became one of the most profitable films in cinema history. The found-footage franchise has since grown to seven installments and grossed more than $900 million globally.

	The new movie stars Chase Yi, Sonia Mena and Maya Da Costa. Peli returns to produce for Solana Films, with James Wan and Jason Blum producing for Blumhouse Atomic. Michael Clear and Judson Scott will executive produce for Blumhouse Atomic, with Alayna Glasthal overseeing the project for the company. Executive producers are Steven Schneider (for Room 101, Inc.), Dan Slater and Cody Calahan. 
	

	More to come…

title: Common Joins Documentary Short ‘The Second Life of Freddie Nole’ as Executive Producer (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Common, the Academy Award, Emmy and Grammy-winning artist and actor, has joined Dana Nachman’s documentary short “The Second Life of Freddie Nole”
body:
Common, the Academy Award, Emmy and Grammy-winning artist and actor, has joined Dana Nachman’s documentary short “The Second Life of Freddie Nole” as an executive producer, Variety can reveal exclusively.  

	According to an official logline, “‘The Second Life of Freddie Nole’ follows an extraordinary man on what initially appears to be an ordinary day. Freddie Nole drives to a Pennsylvania prison to pick up a man who has just been released, offering him a ride, a meal, clean clothes, and something far more valuable: the knowledge that someone is waiting for him. As the vérité road trip unfolds, audiences discover Freddie’s own remarkable history. Sentenced to life in prison at just seventeen years old, Freddie spent nearly fifty years behind bars before regaining his freedom.” 
	

	“The Second Life of Freddie Nole” premiered in June at Tribeca Festival and recently earned a nomination for best short documentary at the 2026 Critics Choice Documentary Awards. Since its debut, the film has  screened at DC/DOX, Raindance London, HollyShorts and the Hamptons International Film Festival.

	“Common has spent years using his platform to advocate for people whose voices too often go unheard,” said Nachman. “What moves me most about Freddie is that he doesn’t just talk about second chances — he shows up at the prison gates and makes them possible. Having Common join our team means the world to us, and we hope together we can inspire more people to help returning citizens reintegrate into our society.”

	 Common is probably best known for starring as Robert Sims in Apple TV’s sci-fi drama “Silo” and for winning the 2015 Oscar for best original song for his work on “Selma.” His recent film credits include “Breathe,” “Fool’s Paradise” and “Alice.” As a musical artist, Common has won three Grammys across 2022 nominations. His standout records include 2000’s “Like Water for Chocolate” and 2004’s “Be.”
	

	“The Second Life of Freddie Nole” will next screen at Firehouse Cinemas at DCTV in New York City on Nov. 10, 2026. Common will be in attendance.

title: Tyler Perry Joins Keisha Lance Bottoms’ Georgia Transition Team Despite Director’s Sexual Assault Lawsuits
description: On Tuesday night, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the 2026 Georgia gubernatorial election, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor
body:
On Tuesday night, Keisha Lance Bottoms won the 2026 Georgia gubernatorial election, making history as the first Black woman to be elected governor of any U.S. state and Georgia’s first Black governor.

	One of the first moves made by Bottoms, who’d previously served as the mayor of Atlanta, a member of Atlanta City Council and a senior advisor and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement under former President Biden, was announcing, “Tyler Perry, an entertainment mogul who is also a huge philanthropic part of our Georgia community and owns Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta,” as part of her transition team.
	


	Bottoms made the announcement during a press conference early Friday, and it’s a controversial pick given the disturbing allegations that the “Madea” filmmaker has faced in recent years.

	Actor Derek Dixon, who’d acted in a number of Perry productions including “The Oval,” filed a lawsuit against Perry in June of last year alleging that Perry had subjected him to numerous instances of sexual battery and assault dating back to 2021. According to the lawsuit, Dixon claims Perry has “been using his power and influence to molest, abuse, and sexually assault impressionable and vulnerable employees and actors who look to him for guidance and mentorship while pursuing their dreams.” Dixon is seeking $260 million in damages and a trial by jury.

	Then, in December 2025, actor Mario Rodriguez, who’d starred in Perry’s comedy-horror film “Boo! A Madea Halloween,” filed a $77 million sexual battery lawsuit against Perry and the film’s distributor Lionsgate accusing Perry of unwanted sexual advices, sexual battery and sexual assault, and that Lionsgate ignored his alleged predation. However, chummy text messages between Rodriguez and Perry after the alleged sexual misconduct later emerged.
	

	Bottoms is set to take office as Georgia’s 84th governor on Jan. 11, 2027.

title: Seville European Film Festival Honors Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Cartoon Saloon
description: Honoring Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon, the Seville European Film Festival bows Friday with a main c
body:
Honoring Agnieszka Holland, Thierry Frémaux and Irish animation studio Cartoon Saloon, the Seville European Film Festival bows Friday with a main competition featuring Dani de la Orden’s “The Director” and Andrew Haigh’s “A Long Winter” and the ambition to capture the genius, true gamut and new talents of Europe’s productions.

	Of Seville’s three 2026 honorees, Holland went first. A towering presence in Polish cinema and a voice of its conscience, Agnieszka Holland (“Angry Harvest,” “Europa Europa”), she wil receive a Golden Giraldillo from the festival. Talking at a Friday press conference, interviewed by Seville European Film Festival Director Manuel Cristobal, she talked about he current state of European cinema. “I think that we should take more risks. We ned courage and freedom to listen to people’s realities, and open up a little more. It’s difficult because the world has changed a lot in he last 10 years with social media, big data and AI. Hard truth has lost its attraction. I’m not very optimistic but we must attempt it.”
	

	Cannes head Thierry Fremaux, who has maintained the event as the most important festival in the world, which is no mean achievement, will also be in Seville to pick up a Giraldillo de Honor, as will Cartoon Saloon, a pioneer of exquisite 2D Irish feature film animation of international market appeal – think 2007’s “The Secret of Kells” – will receive a third. The award corresponds with Cartoon Saloon’s 25th anniversary.

	“One of the wonderful things that festivals can do is pay respect to people that have open roads for European cinema and world cinema,” says Seville European Film Festival Director Manuel Cristobal.
	

	Agnieszka Holland is a New Cinema pioneer, and the award to Thierry Frémaux is not just for heading up the Cannes Festival but also his work at Lyon’s heritage cinema Lumière Film Festival and documentaries on the Lumière brothers. Cartoon Saloon has made great animated faetures and give its its 25th anniversary, we thought: ‘Why not for the first time in he Festival’s history, give a Giraldillo to a company, not a person.”

	Pushing Screenwriting

	Opening with Sébastien Laudenbach’s Cannes animation hit “Viva Carmen!” with Laudenbach and lead voice actress Camélia Jordana attending, Seville guests this year also take in Oscar winner Fernando Trueba with doc feature “Bajañi,” catnip for music lovers, to AMPAS VP Howard A. Rodman best known as a screenwriter of “Savage Grace,” starring Julianne Moore, and “August,” with Josh Hartnett, Rip Torn, and David Bowie, who will head up this war’s Seville fest jury.

	That choice is no coincidence. When the Seville European Film Festival unveiled this year’s main competition lineup, it unveiled roles, their director and their screenwriters. Their role in the collective art of cinema is not appreciated enough, Cristóbal has argued. In the biggest new push at Frame, Seville Festival’s industry umbrella, partnering with Spain’s ICAA film agency. Seville will launch Insula, a screenplay market featuring 58 titles.

	Seville European Festival’s New Talent Drive

	Two of the most awaited titles in Seville’s main competition are most certainly “The Director” and Andrew Haigh’s “A Long Winter.”

	A world premiere, backed by Beta Fiction Spain marking De la Orden’s follow-up to breakout “A House on Fire,” “The Director” is based on David Jiménez’s lid-lifting autobiographical non-fiction book, charting his time trying to lead the digital transformation of newspaper El Mundo, which becomes a record of journalism under pressure from political and economic interests.



	

					‘El Director’
	



	Haigh’s first film since “All of Us Strangers,” “A Long Winter,” set on a farm in the Rockies in the early ’50s, was hailed by Variety as “a sweeping act of cinematic storytelling.”

	De la Orden and Haigh are courted directors. One of Seville’s, most exciting facets is its focus on breakout new talent: One whole section at the festival, Rampa, features first and second features from Europe. Debuts also spangle the Seville European Film Festival’s main competition.
	

	Starring “Vikings’” Gustaf Skarsgård, “Adult Supervision,” the first feature of well-known Swedish author and podcast host Alex Schulman, has sold widely by Heretic, including to WBD, Place and Vertigo.

	Other new talent highlights Serbian Miroslav Terzić “3 Weeks After,” an unflinching portrayal of brutal high-school bullying, and Abinash Bikram Shah’s thriller “Elephants in the Fog,” set in a Nepalese transgender community which won Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize

	Also drawing praise among Golden Giradillo contenders are Eivind Landsvik’s debut “Low Expectations,” a “slow, quiet and life-affirming late coming-of-age tale you don’t want to look away from” driven but its central performance by from Norwegian singer-songwriter-producer Marie Ulven, also known as Girl in Red.

	Another Un Certain Regard title, “Words of Love,” the second feature from Rudi Rosenberg, is described by Variety as a a film which captures sensitively captures the chaos and compassion of family.

	Underscoring the Range of European Cinema

	These new discoveries are joined by the latest films from more established directors such as “Black Money for White Nights,” a probing take on pro-Russia nostalgia from Bulgaria’s Kristina Grozeva and Petar Valchanov, Karlovy Vary Crystal Globe winners with “The Father.”

	Also in contention is The Idiot(s), starring Johnny Flynn and Aimee Lou Wood, an “unexpectedly romantic portrait” of Dostoevsky and his wife from Polish duo Małgorzata Szumowska, an EFA and three-time Berlin winner, and well-known cinematographer Michał Englert.

	Beyond established auteurs, Seville also programs crossover tiles – think no further than “La Bola Negra,” a star title in a European Film Academy panorama which accompanies the announcement of EFA nominations in Seville. In 2025, Seville program Season 6 of “The Chosen.” It sold out in minutes, Cristóbal recalls. This year, one title turns on Seville soccer club.

	“We want to program different films attending the different audiences in Europe. Seville is also the fourth biggest city in Spain, so we ned to expand the scope of the Festival,” says Cristobal.

	Andalusia Calls

	Seville’s main competition also features another first feature, the buzzy “Taranta,” a doc feature directed by Samuel Nacar and produced by Seville-based Sarao Films. It is set in Lnares, once a boom town until its car factory closed. Now it has one of the highest unemployment rates in Europe. “The principal idea is to ask what it’s like to grow up in a town which you think has no future,” says Nacar. Even when a Chinese company reopens the Linares’ local car plant, the film’s two young Spanish protagonists hesitate between staying or leaving.
	

	An Andalusian Panorama gives some idea of the scale of Andalusia’s output – there are 16 titles – and the quality Andalusian productions ca reach, led by the Womack Studios-produced “Bajañi,” in which Fernando Trueba follows flamenco guitarist Niño Josele as he explores jazz and Brazilian music, playing with is greats, such as Caetano Veloso, Ron Carter and Rubén Blades.

title: Leo Reich on Capturing Gen Z Angst in ‘It Gets Worse,’ Scoring a Lena Dunham Cameo and Having ‘Loads of Ideas’ for a Potential Season 2
description:
Leo Reich can’t seem to shake London.

	Born and raised north of the river, the 28-year-old comedian, actor and writer moved east a few years ago —
body:
Leo Reich can’t seem to shake London.

	Born and raised north of the river, the 28-year-old comedian, actor and writer moved east a few years ago — and it’s probably the furthest he’ll venture from home.

	“I wish I could be one of these people who’s like, ‘I’m going to go live in Spain for a year.’ I’m not,” Reich admits at a hip coffee shop around the corner from his flat, sipping on an iced latte despite the dropping temperature. To cope, he’s sporting a red Vivienne Westwood scarf over a simple black jean jacket and white T-shirt.
	

	To his credit, Reich did once try out New York City for a month and a half in the early days of his stand-up career. He’d grown up a fan of movies and shows set in the Big Apple — “Frances Ha,” “Girls,” “30 Rock” — but it didn’t live up to his expectations. “Because I was kind of this pretentious teenager, I was like, ‘I gotta move to New York in my 20s, it’s going to be fucking incredible.’ And then I eventually went and I was like, ‘This sucks.’ They didn’t get me!”

	Luckily, Reich’s hometown has provided the perfect backdrop for “It Gets Worse,” the comedy series he wrote and stars in that also marks A24‘s debut U.K.-made show. “Everyone I’ve ever met is here,” he says of London. “It’s perfect.”

	Judging from our one hour at the coffee shop, this isn’t that much of an exaggeration. Reich is approached twice, once by a friend and once by a stranger, both gushing with praise about “It Gets Worse.” “I haven’t laughed out loud like that in ages!” a 20-something girl excitedly tells Reich. “Amazing work.”

	When we meet, the show has been out in the U.K (via Channel 4) for just six days, but Reich has already been surprised by the enthusiastic reception and rave reviews from The Guardian, The Times and more. And on Friday, it will premiere across the pond on Paramount+. “So far it’s been such a nice, warm reaction for a show that is, I would say, at points really unbearable to watch,” Reich says with a laugh.
	

	Inspired by his favorite American shows, including “Girls,” the comedy follows three best friends and roommates — Ethan (Reich), Abi (Emily Fairn) and Sam (Olive Gray) — as they navigate their 20s in London after moving out of their shared flat. It possesses that dry, awkward, self-deprecating British humor that is clearly shared by its author, along with a healthy dose of pessimism (as is implied by its title). The result is a hilarious, all-too-real depiction of the existential angst that has come to plague Gen Z-ers across the globe. 

	“The show is meant to be about three characters who see themselves as main characters in a TV show about themselves,” Reich explains. “And they’ve grown up watching all of this stuff about how being in your 20s in a big city is mean to look, and they’re failing to do it.”



	

					Abi Fairn, Olive Gray and Leo Reich in “It Gets Worse.”
									Courtesy of Paramount+
	



	Ethan is looking for love in all the wrong places while refusing to look for a job; Abi is doing everything to convince herself to stay in an unfulfilling relationship out of longing for a traditional life; and Sam is a struggling writer who finds herself sharing an apartment — and a lover — with her ex. In short, adulthood isn’t what they thought it would be.

	“It’s this pseudo intellectual, kind of self-aggrandizing thing of, this has to be romantic in some way,” Reich says. “It’s people living for the plot, and it’s like, there is no plot, sweetheart. This is your real life.”

	Was “It Get Worse” based on Reich’s real life? Yes and no. 

	“My friends find it funny when I say it’s not, because they’re like, it obviously is. But it’s not true events,” Reich says. Ethan, Abi and Sam aren’t based on real people, but are instead “sort of different versions of me,” he adds. As for Ethan’s love life: “That’s based off like, 50 people — an amalgamation of some of the most inaccessible kind of bisexual men that I’ve thrown myself at in the most desperate ways. All of whom I’m still friends with.”

	Beyond the three main characters, “It Gets Worse” also features an eclectic ensemble with some of the most impressive cameos in recent TV memory: There’s Andrew Scott as a hot therapist, bestselling author Zadie Smith as the show’s narrator and voice of reason, artist BabyMorocco as a douchey DJ, “Chicken Shop Date” host Amelia Dimoldenberg as an annoyingly nice it-girl and “Inbetweeners” star Blake Harrison as a quirky lodger Ethan’s mom takes in. Reich even recruited “Girls” creator Lena Dunham to play the Millennial girlboss at Abi’s office, who has become — in a plot twist 13-year-old him would not believe — a mentor of sorts.
	

	The two met after Dunham watched a recording of Reich’s breakout Edinburgh Fringe Festival comedy show “Literally Who Cares?!” in 2022 — before it was picked up for HBO Max. “I get a call being like, ‘Lena Dunham’s written a part for you,'” Reich recalls. “I literally fell to the floor. I couldn’t believe it.”

	That part was in “Too Much,” Dunham’s return to TV nearly a decade after “Girls” and love letter to her new life in London. Reich played Boss Gibbons, the painfully Gen-Z co-worker of Megan Stalter’s expat Jessica, in his first-ever screen acting role. “The first time I met her, I was so nervous — two seconds in, I’m screaming laughing,” he says of Dunham. “She’s just the easiest person to be around, and that whole thing was so fun.”

	Naturally, Dunham gave Reich notes on the “It Gets Worse” pilot, and to his surprise, offered to guest star. “She went, ‘Oh, and I’d love to be in it if you want me to be,'” he says. “I was like, ‘What are you talking about?! Do I want you to be in it? Uh, yeah. I’m gonna write a part now.'” 



	

					Lena Dunham in “It Gets Worse.”
									Courtesy of Channel 4
	



	Similar to “Girls,” “It Gets Worse” doesn’t shy away from sex. In fact, there’s an entire storyline based around a sex party gone wrong. But Reich insists he’s not trying to make a “conscious political statement” about sex on screen, despite reports that Gen Z could do without it. 

	“I just think sex is funny,” he says. “It felt to me like there was an era of very clean, sort of idealized sex scenes; almost educational on the one hand, or so eroticized that it becomes not hot on the other hand. Both of those things are great — it’s not, in my experience, how people have sex.”

	Now that the series is premiering in America, Reich is anxious to see if it will be New York City stand-up all over again. (Judging by Variety‘s glowing review, it won’t.) “There is some kind of significant cultural difference in what people find funny intuitively, so that will be interesting,” he says. 

	But Reich is hopeful that “It Gets Worse” will get a chance for a second season — he has “loads of ideas” — just so Ethan and his friends can see how much worse it can actually get.

	“No one’s gonna make it! It’s in the fucking title,” he says with a cackle. “People going, ‘Aw, do they end up together?’ Bitch, read the title of the show. No one gets what they want ever.” 
	

	However, “The worst it could get is if it gets canceled, of course,” he adds, turning slightly serious. “But it was fun while it lasted. There’s a little bit of a badge of honor, I think, for a canceled after one season show. Kind of a cult classic.”

	He’s also eyeing film in the future — maybe a rom-com, though he isn’t picky. “I’d love to do anything. Please, God,” he says. “If this is my job for the rest of my life, I’ll be the luckiest boy in the world.”

title: Adam Driver Explains Why He’s Starring in Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Reboot After Years of Turning Down MCU Offers: ‘Felt Like the Right Time’
description: Adam Driver opened up about why he said yes to playing Mister Sinister in the “X-Men” reboot after turning down many Marvel movies over the years.
body:
Adam Driver opened up about why he said yes to playing Mister Sinister in the “X-Men” reboot after turning down many Marvel movies over the years.

	“I was a big fan [of ‘X-Men]. I mean, I was a fan of the other things too, but this one felt like the right time,” Driver said during a recent appearance on “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” Further reflecting on the reasons he joined the project, Driver added, “It was really ‘X-Men,’ Jake Schreier, who’s the director, his idea for it, and that it’s Kevin Feige. It all kind of came together. The script is really cool.”
	

	Driver explained that he was very selective about joining the MCU because “a lot of people are going to watch it, and if it’s bad, you know, a lot of people will see you being bad. Plus, I don’t want to mess it up.” 

	Marvel head Kevin Feige recently told the “Happy Sad Confused” podcast that he has offered so many Marvel roles to Driver that it has become somewhat of a “tradition” that, when a new project is on the horizon, they meet on Zoom about a part and Driver turns it down. 

	“It’s no secret we’d like to [work with Adam],” Feige said. “But it’s a tradition to Zoom with him and then he passes. That’s a long-lived tradition. He couldn’t be more cordial. He is usually upfront about how he is feeling.”

	In the new “X-Men” film, Driver will play Dr. Nathaniel Essex, aka Mister Sinister, a superintelligent, shape-shifting telepath. As the movie’s main antagonist, he will do battle against Sadie Sink as Jean Grey, Inde Navarrette as Rogue, Kit Connor as Cyclops, Christopher Abbott as Charles Xavier, Maya Boyd as Storm and Asa Germann as Angel.

Macklemore is accusing some of America’s most iconic arenas of shutting his “Free Palestine” tour out.

	The rapper, who recently had dates in Dublin, Paris and London at the end of October, took to Instagram on Nov. 6 to say that he has been turned down by American venues, including New York City’s Madison Square Garden, New Jersey’s Prudential Center, Brooklyn’s Barclays Center, Long Island’s UBS Arena, L.A.’s Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena, San Francisco’s Chase Center and Seattle’s Climate Pledge Arena.
	

	“By mid-September, we received available dates at these arenas through the end of the year,” he said in the Instagram post. “But once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine, those dates were suddenly off the table. The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same. The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues.”

	“In over 20 years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” he also wrote. “I’d rather lose every opportunity in this industry than spend another day protecting people who value their business relationships with Israel more than they value Palestinian human life.”

	“We live in a country that prides itself on freedom of speech. Yet we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome and which human lives are worth defending,” he later wrote. “Today it’s Palestine. What will it be tomorrow?”

	Macklemore ended his post with, “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will. FREE PALESTINE!”
	

	A spokesperson for MSG Entertainment responded to Macklemore’s claims in a statement to Variety: “We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he’s not an arena level act.”

	In September, Macklemore was fired from Ed Sheeran’s “Loop” tour over pro-Palestine comments he made during his opening set at MetLife Stadium. All of the tour’s other openers and Sheeran’s own backing band ended up quitting the tour in solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.

	Variety has reached out to the nine arenas Macklemore mentioned for comment.

	See Macklemore’s full message on Instagram below.

Nov 6, 2026 11:30am PT

	He’s been dissolved at the bottom of the ocean, frozen solid in an iceberg, blown up in a volcano, disintegrated in an atomic meltdown, and killed by missiles on the Brooklyn Bridge, but thanks to the millions of fans who love him, Godzilla will never die. Japan’s biggest star returns again in “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which pits the towering titan against a familiar three-headed rival for their ninth big-screen showdown.

	Like many long-running franchises, the Godzilla series has gone through a number of distinct phases since its introduction. The first phase, which covers the 15 titles released between 1954 and 1975, is commonly known by fans as the Showa era. These kaiju films (kaiju is the Japanese term for giant monster) are marked by their dramatic shift in tone, from the somber and haunting original to the wonderfully ludicrous “Godzilla vs. Hedorah.”

	The second phase is often referred to as the Heisei era, and it includes the seven titles released between 1984 and 1995. These Godzilla films feature a greater sense of narrative continuity, and they ask complex philosophical questions about science and humanity. Next came the Millennium era, which covers the six titles released between 1999 and 2004. The majority of these Godzilla films are self-contained stories, much like an anthology series. The current Reiwa era began with 2016’s “Shin Godzilla” and includes an animated trilogy and the burgeoning Minus series, launched with 2023’s Oscar-winning “Godzilla Minus One.” Meanwhile, Hollywood’s MonsterVerse saga, which kicked off in 2014, continues to chart its own course.

	To help you program the ultimate monster marathon, here’s our Godzilla movie ranking, listed from wretched worst to bestial best. Long live the lizard king!


			
			
	All Monsters Attack (1969)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				The atrocious tenth film in the series focuses on a bullied boy who escapes from his depressing existence by dreaming that he and Godzilla’s moronic son Minilla are playmates on Monster Island. Although helmed by visionary filmmaker Ishiro Honda, who directed many of the best Godzilla films, “All Monsters Attack” is widely regarded as the worst of the worst, and for good reason. Due to budgetary problems, most of the action is comprised of recycled footage from previous Godzilla movies, and the original material looks like it was shot in a single weekend using whatever old monster costumes were on hand. Awful in every way, the American version adds insult to injury by dubbing the childlike Minilla with a deep male voice that sounds oddly like Mr. Ed, the talking horse.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Megalon (1973)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Angered by mankind’s seemingly endless appetite for subterranean nuclear testing (seriously, have these tests ever worked out well for anyone?), an underwater civilization known as Seatopia sends a giant electrified beetle named Megalon up to the surface to stop all the racket. Naturally, Godzilla and his new robotic pal Jet Jaguar defend humanity by throwing foam boulders at the oversized insect. Visually speaking, this unlucky 13th film in the franchise is a drab and gloomy affair, and features some of the dullest monster fighting in the entire series. Much of the blame can be placed on Megalon, who emerges as one of the least charismatic enemies in Godzilla history.
		
			
			
	Son of Godzilla (1967)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Top secret weather control experiments on a tropical island lead to the creation of humungous praying mantises, and only Godzilla and his dopey offspring Minilla can set things right again. Lackluster in all respects, this amateurish eighth entry was directed by Jun Fukuda, the man responsible for some of the silliest – and sloppiest – movies in the franchise. Like a kaiju version of “The Great Santini,” the film portrays Godzilla as a callous and abusive father to his disappointing son, whose creature costume resembles a moldy-looking Pillsbury Doughboy.
		
			
			
	Godzilla (1998)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				This notoriously misguided American reboot appears to have been crafted by filmmakers with little appreciation for what made Godzilla one of cinema’s greatest icons in the first place. Rather than a towering behemoth whose lumbering gait signals the inexorable approach of death and destruction, here we get a scampering, chicken-legged dinosaur who spends most of the movie fleeing from his enemies like a cat running away from a vacuum cleaner. Factor in the film’s leaden humor, bloated running time, and Matthew Broderick’s lifeless performance, and it’s easy to see why this 23rd Godzilla film is loathed by hardcore kaiju fans.
		
			
			
	Godzilla Raids Again (1955)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Notable only for introducing Godzilla’s dog-like adversary Anguirus, who would go on to become one of the most beloved beasts in the series, this rushed production is marred by awkward direction, threadbare special effects, and an interminably slow and meandering second half that dispenses with monster fights in favor of pointless human drama.
		
			
			
	Godzilla 2000 (1999)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				The first film of the series’ newfangled Millennium era, this largely forgettable entry ignores all previous installments and functions as a direct sequel to the original movie. This time, Godzilla battles a UFO that eventually transforms into a lethargic baddie named Orga, whose oversized claws and ungainly body looks suspiciously like the Rancor monster from “Return of the Jedi.” Although the story’s human subplots are better handled than usual this time, “Godzilla 2000” contains only a handful of memorable scenes, making it one of the more skippable titles in the franchise.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. SpaceGodzilla (1994)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				When Mothra accidentally exposes a few of Godzilla’s skin cells to energy from a black hole, a bizarre new creature nicknamed SpaceGodzilla is born and quickly begins terrorizing Earth. Although the idea of Godzilla battling an evil doppelganger is ripe with possibility, this 21st entry does little to distinguish itself and often feels like a retread of familiar moments from better movies. Admittedly, SpaceGodzilla looks extremely cool with massive glowing crystals protruding from his back and shoulders, but his powers are frustratingly random and the movie’s storyline is a bit of a mess. An appearance by the robotic Moguera, first introduced in Toho’s 1957 sci-fi thriller “The Mysterians,” does little to elevate the tired material.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla II (1993)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				When military scientists create a newly improved Mechagodzilla using the remains of the recently defeated Mecha-King Ghidorah, they think they’ve finally found a way to kill Godzilla once and for all. Meanwhile, in a possible nod to “Kramer vs. Kramer,” Godzilla and Rodan duke it out over custody of a recently discovered Baby Godzilla. Although energetically directed by Takao Okawara, this 20th Godzilla film feels a bit old hat. Part of the problem is that with so many excellent Mechagodzilla movies in the series to choose from, this one just doesn’t seem that special. Other than Mechagodzilla’s beefed-up torso, which makes him look a steroid-enhanced gym rat, there’s not a lot that’s new here.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Gigan (1972)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				With his red cyclopean eye, metallic jai alai scoop hands, razor-sharp beak, and dorsal-finned back, the giant alien cyborg named Gigan is one of Toho’s most impressively designed monsters; and that’s before his secret buzzsaw belly-blades are revealed in all their gory glory. Although the film’s plot isn’t quite as inventive, that doesn’t mean there aren’t some genuine pleasures to be had here. In particular, setting the final battle at a monster-themed amusement park complete with a Godzilla-shaped building that fires lasers from its mouth is a welcome touch, as are the grotesque alien cockroaches who set the absurd story in motion.
		
			
			
	Ebirah, Horror of the Deep (1966)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				When a young man and his two friends find themselves shipwrecked on a remote island while searching for a lost brother, they encounter terrorists, enslaved natives, and a ginormous lobster named Ebirah. In the process of avoiding capture, they accidentally awaken Godzilla, who apparently took a disco nap on the island after the events of “Invasion of Astro-Monster.” Less concerned with global cataclysm and world domination, this fun entry in the Godzilla series works well as a standalone story. Although Ebirah doesn’t have many unique abilities – other than being a crustacean the size of a battleship – the monster fights are invigorating and well-staged, and the lush island setting provides a refreshing change of scenery from the endless urban destruction that the franchise usually focuses on.
		
			
			
	Godzilla: Tokyo S.O.S. (2003)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				When Mothra’s miniature fairy minions inform the Japanese government that Godzilla will continue to rain destruction upon Japan unless they destroy Mechagodzilla, the country’s stubborn Prime Minister ignores the dire warnings, setting in motion an epic battle between all three super-sized opponents. While the plot won’t win any awards for originality, director Masaaki Tezuka captures some seriously impressive monster fights in this 27th film in the series. Mothra fans, in particular, will find much to love about this installment, which frequently refers back to the giant moth’s 1961 standalone movie. Even Mothra’s silk-shooting larvae are given a chance to shine by trapping Godzilla in an impenetrable cocoon during the climactic battle. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla (2014)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Featuring an intense performance by Bryan Cranston and a striking new creature design for the title character, this bold reimagining of Godzilla was a monster-sized hit for Legendary Pictures. Unfortunately, Cranston barely makes it through the film’s first act, and Godzilla has even less screen time than he does. The camera work is exquisite… when you can actually see it. Much of the film’s second half is so dimly lit and obscured by smoke and fog, it’s honestly difficult to tell what’s happening during the meager number of monster tussles we’re given. Note to future kaiju filmmakers: the Godzilla series is not “The Blair Witch Project.” The audience has to actually see the onscreen action to appreciate it. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla and Mothra: The Battle for Earth (1992)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Another big treat for longtime Mothra fans, this 19th entry finds Earth itself declaring war on humanity in the form of Battra, a giant black moth who’s revealed to be the physical embodiment of the planet’s inherent instinct for self-protection. Filled with fantastic imagery and thrilling battle scenes, the film was Mothra’s first appearance on screen in 25 years, and director Takao Okawara provides her with a vibrant new look and some freshly super-charged powers. Although Godzilla is given less to do here than he is in most other installments, the addition of Battra, who acts as a dark twin to Mothra, is an inspired touch that makes up for Godzilla’s relative lack of agency in the movie.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah (1991)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				The only Godzilla film to incorporate time travel into its story, this wonderfully weird 18th entry has enough plot to fill a half-dozen movies. In a nutshell, time travelers from the future arrive in the present with a warning that Godzilla will cause an apocalyptic nuclear accident in a few years, and the only way to prevent it is to travel back to World War II and stop him from being created in the first place. But that’s just the tip of the narrative iceberg in this over-the-top extravaganza. None of the film’s time travel rules make any sense whatsoever, but that doesn’t stop this monster mash from being outrageously entertaining. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Megaguirus (2000)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				One of the more underrated entries of the Millennium era, this installment ignores all previous Godzilla films and picks up where the 1954 original left off. When Godzilla emerges from his decades-long slumber, Japan unveils a new weapon capable of firing artificial black holes at the rampaging monster. But during a test run, the weapon accidentally opens a dimensional wormhole, and a giant dragonfly pops through just long enough to deposit an egg in our dimension. Before long, dozens of gargantuan insects and their menacing queen attack Godzilla like a swarm of irradiated locusts. Featuring a beautifully designed enemy in Megaguirus, not to mention a storyline that’s surprisingly easy to follow for a change, this 24th Godzilla movie feels like a welcome return to the early days of the series.
		
			
			
	Godzilla Against Mechagodzilla (2002)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Not to be confused with the similarly titled “Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla,” this 27th entry plays like a trial run for Guillermo del Toro’s “Pacific Rim,” with a human-piloted robot battling a flesh-and-blood monster for control of the Earth. As the lead pilot who operates the newly designed Mechagodzilla, actress Yumiko Shaku delivers a performance that’s powerful enough to make you wish she appeared in more Godzilla movies, rather than just a cameo role in “Godzilla: Tokyo S.O.S.” Longtime Toho fans will appreciate the callbacks to classic kaiju movies of the past, like the original “Mothra” and “War of the Gargantuas,” but it’s Mechagodzilla’s imposing new look – especially those shoulder mounted cannons and segmented neck structure – that leaves the biggest impression.
		
			
			
	Godzilla: King of the Monsters (2019)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				A much-needed course correction after the anemic action of the first MonsterVerse movie, this occasionally dazzling epic features some amazing creature fights, including a sensational aerial battle between Rodan and King Ghidorah. Although the majority of the monster scenes are once again annoyingly obscured by torrential rainstorms and typhoon-level sea surges, the film is an improvement on the previous entry in almost every way. Each of the newly designed monsters is given at least one showstopping moment, making the movie a treat for longtime Godzilla disciples.
		
			
			
	Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire (2024)
			
										
					Image Credit: ©Warner Bros/Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Although Godzilla’s name comes first in the title, the focus is almost entirely on Kong’s journey in this MonsterVerse entry. Much of Godzilla’s screen time is spent absorbing energy in preparation for the climactic fight or napping in Rome’s Colosseum, making him a supporting character here rather than a true co-star. In terms of spectacle, director Adam Wingard swings for the fences, but by going so big, he inadvertently saps the monsters of their intimidating size and scale for long sections of the film. Setting much of the action in the cavernous Hollow Earth makes the Titans look smaller than they actually are. For example, when Kong tussles with a group of giant simians in their underground lair, they basically resemble average size CGI gorillas duking it out, which leaves the movie feeling more like an installment of the Planet of the Apes series than a kaiju film. As for the human cast, Rebecca Hall and Brian Tyree Henry may as well be off-screen narrators explaining the pedestrian plot every few minutes in extended passages of dry exposition. On the plus side, Kong is a remarkably expressive character, his new Power Glove is great, and the psychedelic color palette makes the film look like a ’70s prog rock album cover come to life, especially during an inventive anti-gravity action sequence.
		
			
			
	King Kong vs. Godzilla (1962)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				The first film in the series to be shot in color, this third entry basically embodies the phrase “so bad it’s good.” Freed from the icy tomb he was trapped in at the end of the previous movie, Godzilla emerges ready to confront King Kong, who’s been transported to Japan by a dastardly drug company. A spectacularly wacky addition to Godzilla history, this glorious grudge match between two of cinema’s best-known monsters is stuffed with corny humor and hilariously cheesy fight scenes. Given a spiffy new make-over by returning director Ishiro Honda, Godzilla’s appearance here is truly awesome. Kong, however, doesn’t fare as well. In fact, he looks like someone sculpted a monkey’s face out of mashed potatoes and stuck it on a filthy shag carpet. But that’s just one of the many charming aspects of this bonkers installment.
		
			
			
	Destroy All Monsters (1968)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				When female aliens from planet Kilaak release all of Earth’s kaiju from their confines on Monster Island, it’s up to the United Nations to step in and regain control of the destructive giants. The cinematic equivalent of an all-star WWE pay-per-view event, this madcap monster melee pulls out all the stops when it comes to action and excitement. In addition to familiar creatures like Godzilla, Rodan, Mothra, and King Ghidorah, the movie also includes a number of lesser-known behemoths like leaping lizard Gorosaurus, slithering sea serpent Mandra, and savage spider Kumonga. It’s a no-holds-barred monsterpalooza!
		
			
			
	Godzilla, Mothra and King Ghidorah: Giant Monsters All-Out Attack (2001)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Often referred to simply as “GMK,” this endearing homage to classic Godzilla movies of the past is a fine entry point for new viewers or returning fans who haven’t kept up with the series in a while. Directed by Shûsuke Kaneko, who brilliantly rebooted the moribund Gamera series in 1995, the film doesn’t shy away from showing viewers the painful human cost of the non-stop monster battles that have plagued Earth for decades. Best of all, Godzilla is reimagined here as a terrifying threat for the first time in years. With his disturbing all-white eyes and demonic snarl, the Big G has rarely seemed more frightening. 
		
			
			
	Invasion of Astro-Monster (1965)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				Here’s a valuable tip for you. Never, under any circumstances, trust a race of sunglass-wearing aliens from Planet X when they arrive on Earth asking to “borrow” Godzilla and Rodan for a little while. One of the all-time craziest sci-fi themed entries in the franchise, this sixth Godzilla movie has a lot going for it, especially the welcome presence of American actor Nick Adams, playing a cocky astronaut who shows the pleather-clad extraterrestrials who’s boss. Adams was no stranger to kaiju movies, having costarred in Toho’s giant monster pic “Frankenstein Conquers the World” shortly before appearing in “Invasion of Astro-Monster.”
		
			
			
	Godzilla: Final Wars (2004)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Everett Collection				
					
				This divisive 50th anniversary entry is admittedly overlong and overstuffed, but that’s what makes it so audacious. Tasked with wrapping up Godzilla’s sci-fi heavy Millennium era, director Ryûhei Kitamura throws everything at the screen in an effort to wow audiences and reward lifelong kaiju fans. The result is a wildly entertaining yarn that combines Matrix-style martial arts with loving references to classic movies in the Godzilla franchise. Second-string monsters like Gigan, King Caesar, and Ebirah get stunning upgrades, and the film earns extra points for the way that Godzilla nonchalantly demolishes his American cousin, rebranded here as Zilla. 
		
			
			
	Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster (1964)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				Effortlessly blending serious action and jovial humor, the splendid fifth film in the series did more than just introduce the world to the shimmering gold-scaled dragon named Ghidorah. It actually managed to transform Godzilla from villain to hero for the very first time. Combining ancient prophecies, political conspiracies, and cosmic mumbo jumbo, the movie’s bombastic plot barely holds together, but who cares when there’s this much magic on screen? A prime example of the golden age of kaiju moviemaking, the film’s most dynamic character is, naturally, Godzilla’s magnificent three-headed adversary; a miraculously designed monster whose weird chittering vocal noises nicely compliment his opponent’s iconic roar. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Hedorah (1971)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				When an alien microbe hitches a ride on a meteor and plummets to Earth, it develops a taste for pollution and quickly becomes a towering toxic sludge monster named Hedorah. Godzilla, now a full-fledged defender of humanity, leaps to mankind’s defense and battles the sentient trash heap, whose smell alone can kill people. Many fans might wonder how this indescribably strange 11th film in the franchise managed to rank so high on this list. Well, the answer is simple: there’s literally no other Godzilla movie quite like this surreal curiosity piece. Granted complete creative control, first-time director Yoshimatsu Banno fashions a trippy, nightmarish, and altogether groovy ecological horror film that’s part cautionary tale, part insane kiddie flick. Although Hedorah occasionally resembles a 200-foot pile of dirty laundry, there’s something undeniably compelling about his disgusting design. A genuine camp classic.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Kong (2021)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Entertainment				
					
				
Restoring a sense of joy and wonder to the franchise after the dour first two entries in the MonsterVerse saga, this fast-paced kaiju smorgasbord brims with affectionate tributes to everything from Edgar Rice Burroughs’ pulpy Hollow Earth novels to Toho Studios’ 1967 classic “King Kong Escapes.” Lighter in tone than the three previous movies in this cycle, the story finds the secretive Monarch organization desperately trying to determine why Godzilla has reverted to his old destructive ways. Globetrotting from one colorful continent to the next, the film includes multiple subplots that keep the action moving at a fever pitch, and the jaw-dropping combat scenes between the hulking and immovable Godzilla and the lithe and graceful Kong are some of the best in the series. And then there’s the newly upgraded Mechagodzilla, whose deadly power and threatening design would give Optimus Prime nightmares. The final three-way battle in Hong Kong is a beautifully choreographed skirmish that’s shot to resemble the original Toho Godzilla movies, which gives this installment a massive leg up on “Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire” and its oddly-scaled monster fights.

		
			
			
	The Return of Godzilla (1984)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				After a nine year absence from the big screen, Godzilla roared back into theaters again with this triumphant reboot that blends a disaster movie scenario with a classic kaiju epic. Featuring impressive special effects and gorgeous production values that make it look like a major Hollywood studio film, the first entry in Godzilla’s Heisei era is more grounded than most giant monster movies, which works to its advantage. Godzilla’s breathtaking new look, especially his re-designed head, set the stage for all the future Heisei installments that followed. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla Minus Zero (2026)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				
	Set two years after the events of “Godzilla Minus One,” this immaculately produced sequel interrupts Japan’s postwar recovery with the arrival of another mountainous menace. Boasting awe-inspiring set pieces and extraordinary technical craftsmanship, it’s a worthy follow-up to its Oscar-winning predecessor, though it lacks some of the original’s heartfelt resonance. At times, the film’s overstated approach makes it feel more like a bridge between installments than a fully realized film in its own right. And at 135 minutes, the middle act’s emphasis on military planning makes the long stretches without Godzilla feel borderline sluggish. Even the climactic monster battle seems strangely low-stakes, unfolding in an already devastated wasteland rather than a bustling city. While Ghidorah remains an iconic adversary, recycling the familiar three-headed terror feels like a missed opportunity to introduce a thrilling new creature to the franchise. Still, there’s no denying the spectacular artistry and sheer cinematic ambition on display, and even a slightly underwhelming Godzilla movie can deliver moments of pure, exhilarating magic. In short, it’s a stellar sequel, if not quite a monster-sized masterpiece.
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Biollante (1989)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				Five years after the down-to-earth action of “The Return of Godzilla,” Toho followed things up with the most dreamlike movie in the franchise’s history. The film’s fascinating storyline involves a grief-stricken genetic scientist who creates a monstrous mutation by combining the cells of his deceased daughter with plant DNA and a few of Godzilla’s chromosomes. The horrifying result looks like something David Cronenberg might’ve come up with had he been tapped to direct a kaiju pic. This hugely original entry in the series asks complex philosophical questions about identity and medical ethics. In fact, you could actually remove Godzilla from the plot entirely and it would still be a memorable sci-fi film. Of course, that’s not to say there isn’t plenty of monster-on-monster mayhem on display. Biollante goes through several bizarre evolutionary stages, each one gooier and nastier than the last. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla (1974)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				Second in popularity only to Godzilla himself, Mechagodzilla was introduced to audiences in this wildly imaginative tale, the penultimate entry of the original Showa era. The robotic giant is given the series’ all-time best entrance, as his scaly outer covering dissolves away to reveal a gleaming metallic understructure hidden beneath it. Occasionally resembling a ‘70s James Bond spoof, the film is jam-packed with everything from new monsters – like an adorably fuzzy lion creature named King Caesar – to psychic visions and ape-faced alien invaders. But it’s Mechagodzilla who emerges as the film’s true MVP. Like a mammoth Inspector Gadget, this tin-colored titan is equipped with finger missiles, laser-beam eyes, rocket-powered feet, and a swiveling head that generates an impenetrable force field. 
		
			
			
	Terror of Mechagodzilla (1975)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				Kaiju auteur Ishiro Honda helmed this gritty follow-up to director Jun Fukuda’s playful “Godzilla vs. Mechagodzilla,” and watching the two movies back to back proves just how much one artist’s vision can differ from another’s, even when their work looks remarkably similar on the surface. Containing many of the same visual elements from Fukuda’s film, Honda’s penchant for turning sci-fi action into real-world metaphor is on full display here. The human drama presented in “Terror of Mechagodzilla” is dark and thought-provoking, and set the stage for complex entries like “Godzilla vs. Biollante” that we’d get in the future. 
		
			
			
	Shin Godzilla (2016)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				Highly controversial and deeply disturbing, this one-of-a-kind monster movie brilliantly reimagines Godzilla as a terrifying force of chaos and horror, and portrays him in ways that haven’t been seen before, and probably won’t be seen again. Fans were split on whether the movie was a visionary work of genius or an insulting gimmick that barely qualifies as a true Godzilla movie. Although it remains hugely divisive, if you’re willing to go with it, this fearsome film will take you places in the Godzilla universe that you haven’t been before. The story is a complete reboot, ignoring even the original 1954 movie, and it takes serious risks by echoing the tragic tsunami that struck Japan in 2011. It asks what society might look like if Godzilla actually existed, and the answers it provides aren’t comforting. In short, it’s a pitch black modern masterpiece unlike anything else in the kaiju genre.
		
			
			
	Mothra vs. Godzilla (1964)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				A candy-colored fantasy containing many of the most unforgettable images in Godzilla’s long history, “Mothra vs. Godzilla” exists in a class by itself. In a curious way, this fourth film in the kaiju franchise resembles “Goldfinger,” the third James Bond blockbuster, which was also released in 1964. After all, both movies improved on their predecessors’ formula and set the template for all future entries in the series. Everything about it works perfectly, from composer Akira Ifukube’s devastating score to Eiji Tsuburaya groundbreaking effects to the provocative storyline and the fine lead performances. And tying it all together is Ishiro Honda’s unsurpassed direction. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla vs. Destoroyah (1995)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				It’s impossible to decide what’s most memorable about this final film of the Heisei era. Is it Godzilla’s stunning new “Burning Godzilla” appearance? Could it be the many clever callbacks and references to the original 1954 film? Or maybe it’s the ghastly design of Destoroyah, one of Big G’s all-time scariest opponents? Or perhaps it’s the fact that Godzilla Jr. finally emerges as a decent character? The truth is, it’s all of those things, plus so much more. But what makes this existential epic truly worthy of classic status is its profoundly emotional ending. For the first time in history, you’ll find yourself sobbing in a Godzilla movie as the final credits roll. Compassionately directed by Takao Okawara, “Godzilla vs. Destoroyah” elevates the kaiju genre to the level of Greek tragedy. 
		
			
			
	Godzilla Minus One (2023)
			
										
					Image Credit: Toho				
					
				
	It’s difficult to believe that after nearly 70 years, Japan’s reigning radioactive reptile still has the power to surprise moviegoers. And yet that’s exactly what this instant kaiju classic did when it was released to critical acclaim and commercial success. The film’s powerful human drama is what sets “Godzilla Minus One” apart from all other entries in the series. Taking place between 1945 and 1947, the movie’s primary focus is on the emotional trauma suffered by Japan in the aftermath of WWII. Tackling real-world issues like PTSD and survivors guilt, the film paints a moving portrait of a nation overwhelmed by grief. As for Godzilla, the version seen here is like annihilation personified. An unnatural disaster on two bulky legs, this Godzilla is brought vividly to life by director Takashi Yamazaki and his Oscar-winning team of visual effects artists. Put simply, this is a film for grown-ups that just happens to co-star a 165-foot tall atomic-powered monster.
		
			
			
	Godzilla (1954)
			
										
					Image Credit: Courtesy Everett Collection				
					
				If Godzilla is indeed the king of the monsters, then director Ishiro Honda’s elegiac masterwork is the king of the monster movies. Like a dark fairy tale shot in vérité style by a documentary news crew, this disquieting metaphor for the horrors inflicted on Hiroshima continues to resonate around the world more than six decades after its release. Rendered in stark black and white, and filled with moving performances by legendary actors like Takashi Shimura and Akihiko Hirata, “Godzilla” is a bleak and austere work of art that stands alone in the annals of cinema.

                          Accuser Wants Him Back Behind Bars
body:
Bill Cosby
                          Accuser Wants Him Back Behind Bars
                          ... Over Unpaid $59M
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              November 6, 2026
                            12:00 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Bill Cosby could find himself back in handcuffs ... because one of his sexual assault accusers wants a judge to issue a warrant for his arrest, claiming he's been blowing off court orders related to the massive judgment he owes her ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court documents, obtained by TMZ, Donna Motsinger is asking a judge to hold the disgraced comedian in contempt ... telling the court Cosby's been refusing to cooperate after a jury ordered him to pay her a whopping $59.25 million in her civil sexual assault case.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Donna claims Cosby hasn't paid a single penny of the judgment ... and has ignored demands to turn over information about his finances, including his bank accounts, income and assets.
      

            In fact, she says a judge ordered Cosby on October 9 to cough up the financial information and pay $1,560 in sanctions within 10 days ... but he allegedly did neither.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Now, Donna wants Cosby dragged into court to answer for allegedly blowing off the judge ... and she's asking for a warrant for his arrest if he doesn't show up.
      
    
            And she's not stopping there ... Donna is also seeking up to $1,000 in fines and five days behind bars for each alleged violation, plus $3,284 in attorney's fees and costs. She's even asking for Cosby to be jailed until he complies with the court's orders if he's found in contempt and continues refusing.
      
    
            As TMZ previously reported ... a jury found Cosby liable in March after Donna accused him of drugging and sexually assaulting her in 1972. She was awarded $19.25 million in damages, plus another $40 million in punitive damages.
      
    
            Cosby later tried to get the verdict tossed and secure a new trial ... but in May, a judge rejected his efforts. He appealed the rulings to a higher court, which remains pending.
      
    
            A hearing on Donna's latest request is scheduled for January.

MSG to Macklemore

                              November 6, 2026
                            12:30 PM PST
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Madison Square Garden had a pretty icy response to Macklemore's claims that the arena turned down his "Free Palestine" tour ... basically implying he's not a big enough artist to headline the Garden!
      
    
            An MSG Entertainment spokesperson tells TMZ ... "We have some of the busiest venues in the world with extremely limited availability and he's not an arena level act."
      
    
            Ouch!!!
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Macklemore claimed Friday that nine major U.S. arenas -- including MSG, the World's Most Famous Arena -- refused to host his "Free Palestine" tour after three sold-out shows in Europe.
      

            The rapper claimed the venues turned him away after learning that the shows would be a benefit for Palestine.
      
    
            The rapper also said the arenas were threatened by the words "Free Palestine" because they "challenge the systems of power they built their fortunes on."
      
    
            While MSG -- and 8 other arenas -- denied him, Macklemore said he and his fans had the option to "build our own stages" ... so who knows which new venues might host his concerts in the U.S. down the line.
      
    
            Before Macklemore tried to extend his "Free Palestine" tour in the U.S. ... the shows sold out in Dublin, Paris and London, so the demand seems to be there!
      
    
            Macklemore was famously ousted from Ed Sheeran's tour over pro-Palestine remarks he made in 2 New Jersey concerts ... sparking widespread backlash and leading to all of Ed's other opening acts quitting the tour.
